newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sceptical Berlin finally sees govt move due in 1999.
newsitem.headline: Sceptical Berlin finally sees govt move due in 1999.

text.p: Berlin breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday after the long-awaited groundbreaking ceremony for a new chancellery finally convinced it Germany's government was determined to move to its new capital soon.

Photographs of Chancellor Helmut Kohl shovelling the first clumps of dirt at the site near the Reichstag parliament building were splashed across newspaper frontpages and headlines announced: "He's a Berliner now!"
Commentators also saw the short ceremony on Tuesday as the point of no return for the historic move, which was decided in 1991 and now looks set to take place in 1999.
"With the groundbreaking for this house of democracy, the last brakes on the move have been torn away," the Berliner Morgenpost daily commented.

"Now even the last daydreamers down in the bowels of the Bonn bureaucracy can no longer deny that they will have to leave their cozy Bonn doll's house by the end of 1999 at the latest and settle down in this quirky metropolis."
Berliners have fretted about their city's future ever since Bonn ignored East German pleas to move the government here as part of the Unity Treaty merging East and West Germany in 1990.

The West German side agreed Berlin would be the official capital, but insisted parliament should decide whether the government should move back to the Prussian city that was the centre of the first united Germany from 1871 to 1945.

After Berlin unexpectedly won by a narrow margin in a 1991 vote, the shocked pro-Bonn lobby gritted its teeth and dragged its feet in every way it could. It looked set to defend its turf, even though Bonn was keeping half of all ministries.
Alarming studies appeared with estimates showing the "real cost" of the move up to five times higher than the eventual 20 billion mark ($12 billion) price tag.
Kohl's cabinet ministers didn't help either. They all turned up their noses at East Berlin's shabby buildings with their 1950s decor and wanted brand new ministries built.

The politician overseeing the move, Construction Minister Irmgard Schwaetzer, was a Bonn supporter with little enthusiasm for the move. Only in late 1994, when Kohl replaced her with Klaus Toepfer, did the project finally seem to get moving.

Toepfer scrapped the ministers' grand building plans and persuaded the foreign ministry to use Berlin's most unloved office block, the squat building that once housed Hitler's Reichsbank and then the communist party's Central Committee.
Even so, there was enough building going on in Berlin to fill the skyline with construction cranes and drive motorists mad because of all the road repair work going on.
But Berliners still kept doubting. An official report last month saying that most ministries had not yet charted detailed plans for the move prompted anxious headlines here.

More proof of Kohl's will to see the move happen in 1999 came last month, though, when he agreed the State Council Building -- home of East Germany's former collective presidency under the late Erich Honecker -- could be used as a temporary chancellery if the new building is not ready on time.
The lobby is adorned with murals showing heroic workers in classic socialist realist fashion -- hardly the place a conservative like Kohl would use if he could avoid it.
"In my wildest dreams, I never thought I'd have an office in that building," he joked with journalists on Tuesday, adding: "I have no worries about any ghosts there."
